projects.name: Orbis Generative Art
projects.description: The procedural particle system uses equations to draw cosmic shapes and then animate them
projects.fullDescription:
This project explores the emerging complexity and entropy of systems in beautiful mathematical ways.

 The math layout is as follows:

 pick an arbitrary starting point s₀ in ℝ². The first ~20 iterations get discarded because you're not yet on the attractor — you're just letting the chaos game \"settle in.\"\n\n2 
 At each iteration, the program randomly picks one of N weighted transform functions fᵢ and applies it: sⱼ = fᵢ(sⱼ₋₁). Each function is an affine transform of the form F(x,y) = (ax + by + c, dx + ey + f). This controls the rotation, scaling, and shear from a 6-parameter matrix 

 The nonlinear variation functions this causes the divergence from the main paths and the quote streakiness. Applying one or more nonlinear variations Vₙ(x,y) gives other effects to it.

 Log-density accumulation. Instead of plotting each point directly, you maintain a histogram: each pixel keeps a hit count. You run millions of iterations and accumulate. The flame algorithm solves the problem of high-density areas clipping by using a logarithmic map from density to brightness, so brightness = log(hit_count).

lastly is the filters and colouring over it, which is just changing the colours, but it does make them look very cool.

projects.name: Easel
projects.fullDescription:
This project was the most complex thing I had ever made at the time, and so the first step was to model the entire thing in Blender. You may ask " ??? Why Blender of all programs? The main reason is the ability to use SVG as UV maps to make variable height engravings and then export them to Fusion for tool paths and then G code. ( see Image 1)

After I had my models and tool path, I then had to wrangle with the awful thing that is Home Depot lumber. Warped and prone to splitting, it took many hours to get things planed down and attached fully straight. (See Image 2)

Next came the CNC. I couldn't just engrave the long parts as they were too long to fit into the machine, and if I messed up once Id have to create an entire new part. The solution to this is engraved panels; this way, I could make a bunch of uniform ones and throw away the ones that I needed to zero in my cuts. Although taking more tries than I thought it got it down to a science and had over 20 nearly identical engraved panels. (see Images 3 and 4)

After this, I realized you couldn't see the engraving very much as it didn't contrast with the wood around it. I applied a coat of lacquer over them all and then used a hand plane to remove the coat from the top, leaving only the sunken area coloured. (See Image 5)

I did the same process for the base to hold the painting, only I had one attempt at the CNC, and I got it. Only after did my hubris kick in, and I decided I wanted to go just a smidge deeper. To my horror, when I returned a second time, it had all been shifted 3cm left. But it was still salvageable, and as I stared at it more and more, I realized it looked.... good. So quickly I covered the top in resin this time, let it dry, planed it off, and wow, it looks phenomenal. My mistake had been remedied. ( See Image 6)

All that was left was assembly, and when all put together, you get this ( See Image 7)

writing.title: Generative Systems and Emergent Complexity
writing.summary: Exploring how simple rules and iterative processes create intricate patterns, from particle physics to organizational design.
writing.content:
Generative systems represent one of the most fascinating intersections between mathematics, art, and engineering. At their core, they embody a simple principle: from basic rules and iterative processes emerge intricate, often unpredictable patterns that rival the complexity found in nature itself.

Consider the formation of a snowflake. Each crystal grows according to simple physical laws—temperature, humidity, and molecular bonding. Yet the result is a unique, infinitely complex structure that no two snowflakes share. This is emergence in its purest form.

In my work with generative art and procedural systems, I've come to appreciate how this principle scales across domains. Whether designing particle attractors for visual effects, optimizing manufacturing processes, or modeling organizational behavior, the underlying truth remains: simple rules, applied iteratively, generate emergent complexity.

The Orbis project exemplifies this philosophy. A few parameters—attraction strength, particle mass, damping coefficients—combined with basic physics simulation, produce mesmerizing orbital structures that appear intentionally designed, yet emerge entirely from mathematical principles.

This approach has profound implications for engineering. Rather than attempting to specify every detail of a system, we can define the rules and let emergence do the work. It's a shift from top-down design to bottom-up generation, and it opens possibilities we're only beginning to explore.

writing.title: Engineering Co-op: Lessons in Process Optimization
writing.summary: Reflections from four months in industry: what academic theory doesn't teach you about real-world problem-solving and team dynamics.
writing.content:
Four months in industry taught me more about real-world engineering than four years of coursework ever could. Not because the theory was wrong, but because it was incomplete—stripped of context, constraints, and the messy reality of working within existing systems.

My co-op focused on process optimization in a manufacturing environment. The academic version of this involves elegant mathematical models, constraint programming, and optimal solutions. The real version involves legacy systems, political considerations, and the question: "Can we actually implement this by Friday?"

One project stands out. We were tasked with reducing waste in a production line. The textbook approach would be to model the entire system, identify bottlenecks, and propose a comprehensive redesign. Instead, I spent the first two weeks simply observing and talking to operators. They knew where the problems were—they lived with them daily.

The solution wasn't elegant. It involved a spreadsheet, three email alerts, and a color-coded printout posted next to each station. It reduced waste by 18% in the first month. It was nothing like what I'd learned in optimization class, and it worked.

This taught me that engineering isn't just about finding the best solution—it's about finding the best solution that can actually be implemented, maintained, and improved by real people in real conditions. Theory provides the foundation, but wisdom comes from understanding the gap between the model and the world.

writing.title: The Chemistry of Soap: Saponification and Molecular Design
writing.summary: A deep dive into the chemistry of soap production, surfactant behavior, and the surprising elegance of amphiphilic molecules.
writing.content:
Soap is one of humanity's oldest and most elegant chemical solutions. For millennia, we've been creating amphiphilic molecules—compounds with both hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions—without fully understanding the molecular choreography that makes them work.

The chemistry is deceptively simple. Saponification is the reaction between a fat or oil (triglyceride) and a strong base (traditionally lye). The base breaks the ester bonds, releasing glycerol and creating fatty acid salts—soap. But the elegance lies in what happens next, at the molecular level.

A soap molecule has a hydrophobic tail (the fatty acid chain) and a hydrophilic head (the carboxylate group). In water, these molecules spontaneously arrange themselves into spheres called micelles, with hydrophobic tails pointing inward and hydrophilic heads facing outward. This structure is the key to soap's cleaning power.

When you wash your hands, soap micelles surround oil and dirt particles, with their hydrophobic tails embedding into the contamination and their hydrophilic heads facing the water. The result: oily contaminants become suspended in water and wash away. It's molecular-scale engineering.

What fascinates me most is how this ancient craft has been refined through chemistry. Modern soap formulations optimize for hardness, lather, skin compatibility, and environmental impact by carefully selecting different fats and additives. The fundamental chemistry remains unchanged, but the sophistication of application has grown exponentially.

This is a reminder that sometimes the most powerful solutions are those that work with natural principles rather than against them. Soap doesn't fight water; it partners with it at the molecular level.
